skills.name: Identifying argument parts in a passage

note.text: A whole passage can mix background, a quoted view, a reason and a qualified conclusion. Identify whose claim each sentence expresses. Preserve terms such as may, not established and only: dropping them can strengthen or reverse the conclusion. Rejecting a proposed proof does not prove its opposite. Reconstruct the offered support before judging whether it succeeds. An argument map should show the role of each relevant claim rather than merely copying the passage in order.

sections.heading: Your goal and connections
sections.text: By the end, you should be able to reconstruct a qualified conclusion and its supporting reason without adding a stronger claim. Builds on: argument roles, indicators and transformation limits. Leads to: later assessment of syllogisms and argumentative prose.

sections.heading: Read the original model
sections.text: Original passage: During a fictional discussion, Manka says that a badge alone does not prove someone is a voter. The rule says every voter has a badge, but other people may also have one. She does not claim that no badge holder votes. Reconstruction: the rule permits badges beyond voters; therefore badge possession alone does not establish voter status. The discussion setting is background.

sections.heading: Apply and check
sections.text: Mark the central qualified claim, list the relevant reasons and keep contextual or quoted material distinct. Paraphrase faithfully, then test support. State whether the conclusion rejects an inference, asserts a fact or recommends an action.

cards.idea: A correction must preserve scope, terms and assumptions.
example: The conclusion says no badge holder can ever vote. Correction: That changes lack of proof into a universal exclusion.
A possible extra badge holder proves every badge holder is a non-voter. Correction: A possibility defeating an inference does not prove that opposite universal.
Every quoted view must be endorsed by the writer. Correction: A passage can report a view to question it.
Reordering an argument permits inventing stronger premises. Correction: Reconstruction clarifies existing support rather than fabricating it.

pick.q: At an imaginary club discussion, a speaker says: We should not infer that Bih belongs to the club voters class merely from membership in the predicate class. Our actual rule is only that all club voters are badge holders. Knowing that Bih is among badge holders does not exclude other kinds of badge holders. What is the speaker’s central conclusion?
pick.r: Membership of badge holders alone does not establish that Bih belongs to club voters.
w: All badge holders are club voters.
Bih definitely cannot belong to club voters.
Every detail about the discussion is an offered logical premise.
e: That is the very reversed rule being rejected.
Failure to establish membership does not establish non-membership.
Setting details need not support the target claim.
pick.y: The passage rejects an inference while leaving the actual membership open.
